task.title: Study Forensics: Novel cholesterol drug dramatically lowers LDL but cardiovascular outcomes unknown
task.prompt: A pharmaceutical company announced results from its Phase 2 trial of a new injectable cholesterol-lowering agent. The drug reduced LDL cholesterol by 65 percent in patients with familial hypercholesterolaemia who were already on maximum statin therapy. Company executives described the results as a major breakthrough in cardiovascular protection and said the drug would transform outcomes for patients at high risk of heart attack and stroke. They announced plans for an accelerated approval pathway based on the LDL reduction data. The trial measured only lipid levels and liver safety over twelve weeks; no cardiovascular events were tracked and no outcomes trial is expected to report for at least four more years.
task.context:
A pharmaceutical trial showing dramatic improvement in a surrogate biomarker
(LDL cholesterol) with the company actively framing the biomarker success as
cardiovascular protection. No clinical outcomes data exist. The rhetorical
leap from biomarker to clinical benefit is explicit and central.
task.reference_solution: The summary describes a drug that dramatically lowers LDL cholesterol (a biomarker) but has not been tested for cardiovascular outcomes (heart attacks, strokes). Despite this, the company actively frames the LDL reduction as "cardiovascular protection" and a "breakthrough" that will "transform outcomes." The claims about clinical benefit are unsupported by the trial data, which measured only lipid levels.

functional_descriptions: LDL reduction is a surrogate marker, not a clinical outcome
company frames biomarker success as proven clinical benefit

common_errors: accepting LDL reduction as sufficient evidence of cardiovascular protection
task.diagnostic_focus: Can the agent identify that a dramatic surrogate biomarker improvement framed as cardiovascular protection is overclaim?
task.gold_summary: Pharmaceutical company actively frames surrogate biomarker improvement (65% LDL reduction) as cardiovascular protection despite no outcomes data. Relabeled from mechanism_vs_evidence to overclaim after calibration sprint confirmed the active rhetorical selling is the primary issue.

gold_evidence_spans.span: Company executives described the results as a major breakthrough in cardiovascular protection and said the drug would transform outcomes for patients at high risk of heart attack and stroke
gold_evidence_spans.why_it_matters: Explicitly frames biomarker success as clinical benefit — the defining overclaim.

gold_evidence_spans.span: The trial measured only lipid levels and liver safety over twelve weeks; no cardiovascular events were tracked
gold_evidence_spans.why_it_matters: Confirms that no clinical outcomes were measured, making the cardiovascular protection claim unsupported.

gold_evidence_spans.span: The drug reduced LDL cholesterol by 65 percent
gold_evidence_spans.why_it_matters: Dramatic surrogate improvement that is rhetorically inflated into clinical claims.

gold_evidence_spans.span: no outcomes trial is expected to report for at least four more years
gold_evidence_spans.why_it_matters: Evidence for clinical benefit will not exist for years, yet claims are made now.

task.gold_justification:
v0.6.5 relabel from mechanism_vs_evidence to overclaim. All three models
(Haiku, Sonnet, Opus) independently classified this as overclaim in the
Mechanism Calibration Sprint 2, with strong reasoning: the company claims
"major breakthrough in cardiovascular protection" and that the drug will
"transform outcomes for patients at high risk of heart attack and stroke"
based solely on 12-week LDL reduction data with no cardiovascular events
tracked. This is textbook overclaim — the conclusion (cardiovascular
protection) goes far beyond the results (lipid lowering). The empirical
finding from multiple sprints confirms: when biomarker success is actively
sold as clinical benefit, models correctly see overclaim, not a
mechanism-evidence gap. The mechanism-vs-evidence framing requires that
the gap between mechanism and evidence is the central issue; here, the
central issue is the rhetorical inflation of claims beyond data.
task.gold_alternative_reading:
One could argue this is mechanism_vs_evidence because the underlying issue
is a surrogate-to-clinical-outcome gap. However, the active rhetorical
selling ("breakthrough in cardiovascular protection", "transform outcomes")
makes overclaim the more precise label. The mechanism-evidence gap is
present but secondary to the overclaim.
task.curator_notes:
v0.6.5 RELABELED. Originally designed as Shape B of mechanism_vs_evidence
(biomarker success sold as clinical benefit). After Mechanism Calibration
Sprint 2, all 3 models (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus) independently classified as
overclaim. Key insight: the Biomarker-to-Clinical shape does NOT produce
mechanism_vs_evidence when the framing is actively promotional. It produces
overclaim. This is now a clean overclaim case that tests whether models
identify surrogate-endpoint inflation. The mechanism_vs_evidence category
is empirically limited to animal/preclinical-to-human gaps (Shapes A, C).
